caption: What if Earth had rings like Saturn? Saturn's rings stretch about 270,000 km across, yet are often only about 10 metres thick. They're mostly water ice, in pieces from dust grains to chunks as big as a house. To get rings, a space rock has to come so close that a planet's gravity tears it apart. From India, Earth's rings would arch across the southern sky every night, climbing higher the further south you go: almost overhead in Kanyakumari, and just a thin edge-on line from the equator. Their shadow would fall on the winter half of the planet, making winters colder. Edge-on rings almost vanish: Saturn's 'disappeared' from our view in March 2025. Plot twist: a 2024 study suggests Earth may have had a ring about 466 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs. Want to see real rings? Shani (Saturn) is in the evening sky this month. Would YOU want rings in your sky? 👇
